events.summary: All three round-1 blockers are now closed with direct telemetry. (1) H1-vs-H2 direction: market-data-service request_rate is flat across onset (967.22/985.77 req/s vs 878.88-1044.69 baseline, whole-window mean 951.56, F25/F26), while CPU steps 44.85% -> 90.0% at 13:22Z at unchanged throughput and memory shows no buildup (F27, F30). With H2's load-surge first hop directly measured and refuted, the two hypotheses no longer share the same observable facts; only H1 explains CPU doubling at constant QPS. (2) The redis trigger is no longer an unverified assumption: logs give a discrete event - redis-cache-2 failing 3 consecutive PING checks at 13:22:10Z and promotion of redis-cache-3 at 13:22:52Z with an explicitly EMPTY dataset (F34) - and 120s-resolution hit_ratio confirms the collapse starts in the 13:22Z bucket (95.9% at 13:20Z -> 10.82% at 13:22Z, F35), not in 13:16-13:20Z. That rules out eviction/memory-pressure as trigger (evictions flat 1.96-4.13/min F31, memory 65-75% then collapse to 6.0% F32, connected_clients 311->40 F33) and matches the mechanism in market-data-service's own logs (F28). (3) The 'no change precedes onset' claim is now robust: the partial deployment listing was re-run clean with the same count (F2), and exchange-gateway and order-service got individual zero-change/zero-deploy checks (F21/F22), closing the scope gap. Scope checks out: redis-cache is the only shared:true node on both ailing services' paths (F5/F23), exchange-gateway stayed flat at 127-136ms (F16), pricing-engine CPU flat (F12), so H3/H4 remain contradicted. Residual uncertainty is confined to a secondary detail - the sub-cause inside redis-cache-2 (OOM/host/network) and whether any redis host telemetry exists - which changes the deeper origin narrative but not the ranked origin or the fix (restore/repopulate cache, fix failover-to-empty-replica behavior). Confidence capped at 0.82: one hop (miss storm -> CPU saturation) is still an inference from co-timing rather than a pre/post controlled comparison, and the only evidence for the empty-dataset premise is a log line plus inferred memory/clients collapse (no keyspace_size metric exists, F37).

tasks.objective: Establish the symptom onset and blast radius. From query_metrics/query_logs, determine when pricing-engine p99 first exceeded its baseline (before 13:30?) and whether the degradation is isolated to pricing-engine or co-occurs in adjacent services (quote cache, API gateway, market-data feeds, downstream callees). Characterize the error signature: are deadline-exceeded errors originating in pricing-engine itself, or are pricing-engine deadlines the result of a slow downstream call? Report per-service latency/error onset timestamps and whether resource metrics (CPU/mem/connections/GC) at pricing-engine show saturation.
tasks.answer: pricing-engine's p99 and error rate first degraded in the 13:20Z bucket (p99 60ms -> 1143ms avg / 2227ms max; errors 0.29% -> 1.27%), i.e. before the 13:30Z report, and the blast radius is not isolated: api-gateway and market-data-service hit their own latency/error jumps in the same 13:20Z bucket (api-gateway p99 ~202ms -> 1271ms; market-data-service p99 ~40ms -> 977ms). The pricing-engine error signature is exclusively 'quote computation deadline exceeded: market-data-service took <n>ms' (first at 13:23:57Z, durations up to 8456ms), indicating pricing-engine deadlines are the result of slow market-data-service calls rather than an internal pricing-engine stall, and pricing-engine CPU stayed flat (~40%, max 44.48%) throughout, showing no local saturation.

tasks.objective: Find what changed around the onset. Use get_deployments and get_config_changes across ALL services (not just pricing-engine) in the window 2026-04-09T11:00Z–14:59Z. Map pricing-engine's dependency graph with get_service_dependencies to identify shared components (caches, gateways, message buses, market-data sources) that pricing-engine depends on and that other services also use. Check search_historical_incidents for prior quote-latency/deadline-exceeded incidents and their root causes.
tasks.answer: In the 11:00–14:59Z window there was exactly one deployment anywhere (auth-service v7.2.0 at 11:30Z, still live, not rolled back) and zero config/flag changes across all services. pricing-engine's graph shows its only shared dependency is redis-cache, which it shares with market-data-service, and market-data-service additionally depends on exchange-gateway. No deployment or config change to pricing-engine, market-data-service, redis-cache or exchange-gateway is recorded, so no change-history evidence explains the quote latency.

tasks.objective: Correlate the leading candidate changes/dependencies from task b against the exact onset time from task a. Specifically: for any deployment/config change or shared-component identified in b, test whether its timing precedes the latency onset and whether its scope matches the observed blast radius. Also check whether the slow component shows its own resource saturation or downstream errors at onset.
tasks.answer: The leading candidate is the shared redis-cache: at the exact 13:20Z onset its hit_ratio collapses from ~95.5% to 45.09% (then 13.04%), and market-data-service — which shares redis-cache and sits directly on pricing-engine's dependency path — shows its own CPU saturating (45.78% -> 72.72% avg / 93.99% max, and 90% in the 13:22Z 2-min bucket) in the same bucket as the latency jump. Timing precedes/coincides with the latency onset, so redis-cache is timing-consistent as the leading candidate; exchange-gateway and pricing-engine CPU show no saturation. I could not complete request_rate/evictions queries (call budget exhausted), so I cannot fully confirm the causal direction (whether cache degradation drove market-data load or vice versa).

tasks.objective: For market-data-service, pull request_rate (QPS/throughput) and memory_pct at 1-2 min resolution over 13:10-13:30Z and compare against the 12:00-13:10Z baseline. Determine whether request volume spiked at the 13:20Z onset or stayed flat while CPU saturated (CPU already known: 45.78% -> 72.72% avg / 93.99% max in the 13:20Z bucket). Flat volume + CPU saturation supports H1 (extra work from cache-miss recomputation); a sharp volume spike supports H2 (capacity saturation from load surge — currently unevidenced and automated-check flagged).
tasks.answer: market-data-service request volume stayed FLAT across onset: request_rate at the 13:19-13:21Z buckets spanning the 13:20Z onset was 967.22 / 985.77 req/s against a 12:00-13:10Z baseline mean of ~951 req/s (range 878.88-1044.69), with no step change; memory_pct was likewise flat (~60-65%). So the CPU step from ~45% to ~90% at 13:22Z occurred at unchanged throughput. This supports H1 (cache-miss-driven recomputation added CPU work per request) and contradicts H2 (no load surge); market-data-service's own WARN logs name the mechanism: 'cache miss storm: quote:<n> not in redis-cache, rebuilding from exchange feed snapshot', 37 matches, first seen 13:22:25Z.

tasks.objective: For redis-cache, pull evictions_per_min, memory_pct/used_memory, keyspace size, connected_clients, and any restart/failover/replication-status signal over 13:10-13:30Z. Determine whether eviction or memory pressure spiked at 13:16-13:20Z (confirming H1's internal-redis-fault assumption and identifying its trigger) or whether keyspace/connected_clients churn indicates changed access patterns downstream (favoring H2). This is the only telemetry that can validate or refute H1's redis-internal-fault premise, which currently rests on zero runtime data.
tasks.answer: redis-cache shows NO eviction or memory-pressure spike at 13:16-13:20Z: evictions_per_min is flat at 1.96-4.13/min across 13:10-13:30Z, memory_pct is steady ~65-75% until 13:21Z, and connected_clients is steady ~288-332 until 13:21Z. Instead, the cache undergoes a hard failover: at 13:22:10Z the primary fails 3 consecutive PING timeouts, at 13:22:52Z a replica is promoted with an EMPTY dataset, and memory_pct/connected_clients collapse (74.63%->6.0%, 311->40) while hit_ratio_pct falls from ~96% to ~11%. So the evidence refutes the "eviction/memory-pressure" trigger for H1 and instead points to an internal redis-cache primary failure + empty-replica promotion as the trigger (matching HIST-107's pattern), with the hit-ratio collapse being a consequence of the empty dataset, not of eviction. The keyspace/connected_clients churn is a downstream client-reconnect storm (15k-93k new connections/10s from 13:30Z), not evidence of changed access patterns driving the fault (which would favor H2).

tasks.objective: Check for any redis-cache-side operational event in-window: config reload/maxmemory-policy change, replica promotion or failover, planned maintenance, or node replacement around 13:16-13:20Z (beyond the already-zero get_config_changes result). Also individually confirm whether exchange-gateway and order-service had any config change in the window, closing the residual gap that these were never separately checked and underpinning the 'no change precedes onset' claim.
tasks.answer: No redis-cache-side operational event is visible in change history: get_config_changes returned zero for the all-services scope (attempted again for 13:00–13:30Z, partial:false) and get_deployments returned zero for redis-cache in that window. exchange-gateway and order-service each independently returned zero config changes and zero deployments, closing the residual gap — there is no config/deployment event on any service preceding the 13:20Z onset. Historical lead HIST-107 ("Cold cache storm after redis failover", root cause "Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica") is explicitly a lead, not evidence, and no failover signal was found for this incident.

critiques.summary: The chain pricing-engine <- market-data-service is solidly verified (F9/F10/F15: only error signature names market-data-service; co-onset 13:20Z; pricing-engine CPU flat F12). But the hop from redis-cache hit-ratio collapse to market-data-service CPU saturation is NOT established: it is an inference in both directions. H1 and H2 share the SAME observable onset facts and diverge only on the direction of causation (cache-miss storm driving market-data load vs. request surge driving both CPU saturation and cache miss churn). The one metric that would separate them (market-data-service request_rate) was never obtained, and the automated check flags H2's volume-surge hop as unevidenced. Two cheap, obtainable observability queries plus one dependency query can separate H1 from H2, so this is not "inconclusive". Also note two scope/data-quality issues: confidence 0.52 for H1 rests on F17 (redis CPU flat) being used to "exclude CPU" while simultaneously asserting the redis fault is internal (eviction/memory/failover) with zero redis runtime telemetry; and the "no change precedes onset" claim (H1/H4 rejection) rests on a once-partial deployment listing and no individual config-change check for exchange-gateway/order-service.

challenges.issue: The central hop 'redis hit-ratio collapse -> market-data CPU saturation' is unverified: no redis runtime telemetry (evictions_per_min, memory_pct, keyspace, connected_clients, replica/failover status) was ever retrieved. F17 only shows redis CPU is flat, which rules out host CPU but does not distinguish an internal redis-side fault from load-driven miss churn. Without this, H1 and H2 are indistinguishable at the onset bucket they share.

Absence of eviction/memory evidence is being inferred from an incomplete metric set, while the assumption text already asserts the fault is 'internal (eviction pressure, replica/failover, memory)' - that is an assumption, not a verified finding, and it carries the top hypothesis.

H2's first hop (request-volume surge) was never queried - budget exhausted - and the automated check flags it as unevidenced. H2 is therefore not actually tested, only ranked lower by preference; if a volume spike exists, H2 explains the same onset facts with a non-fixable 'capacity' root cause, which changes the remediation.

Causality direction between redis hit-ratio collapse and market-data CPU saturation is unresolvable at 4-min bucket resolution (both land in the 13:20Z bucket, F18). H1 asserts redis first; nothing verified establishes precedence even though redis does precede in one sub-bucket claim (96.34 within-bucket max vs 45.09 avg) that is itself within-bucket, not cross-service ordering.

Rejection of the only in-window change rests partly on a deployment listing that was once partial (F2) and on config-change checks that were never run for exchange-gateway/order-service (stated gap). Small but real residual risk of a missed change.

Rejection is well grounded (F9 explicit downstream attribution, F12 flat CPU), but pricing-engine memory/GC/pool metrics were never obtained; acceptable as a rejection given the explicit log attribution, but 'internal stall fully excluded' should not be overstated.

Stated confidence 0.52 for H1 vs 0.28 for H2 is not justified by evidence - both rest on the same verified onset facts with the differentiator unqueried. The ranking reflects preference, not measurement.

evidence_requests.question: For market-data-service, pull request_rate (and QPS/throughput) at 1-2 min resolution over 13:10-13:30Z and compare with the 12:00-13:10Z baseline. Did request volume spike at onset, or was volume flat while the service saturated? Also report market-data-service memory_pct over the same window.
evidence_requests.rationale: This single series discriminates H1 from H2: flat volume + CPU saturation means the extra work came from cache-miss recomputation (H1); a sharp volume spike means capacity saturation from load (H2). H2's volume hop is currently unevidenced and automated-check flagged.

evidence_requests.question: For redis-cache, pull evictions_per_min, memory_pct/used_memory, keyspace size, connected_clients, and any restart/failover/replication-status signal over 13:10-13:30Z. Did eviction or memory pressure spike at 13:16-13:20Z, or did cache writes/keys churn instead?
evidence_requests.rationale: Establishes whether the hit-ratio collapse originates inside redis (eviction/memory/failover => H1 confirmed and its trigger identified) or is a downstream consequence of changed access patterns (=> favors H2). Currently H1's redis-internal-fault assumption has zero telemetry behind it.

evidence_requests.question: Check for any redis-cache-side operational event or change in-window: config reload / maxmemory-policy change, replica promotion or failover, planned maintenance, or node replacement around 13:16-13:20Z (beyond the already-zero get_config_changes result), and confirm whether exchange-gateway or order-service had any config change in the window.
evidence_requests.rationale: Identifies a concrete trigger on the redis side to convert H1's assumption into evidence, and closes the stated residual gap that exchange-gateway/order-service config changes were never individually checked, which underpins the 'no change precedes onset' claim.

critiques.summary: All three round-1 blockers are now closed with direct telemetry. (1) H1-vs-H2 direction: market-data-service request_rate is flat across onset (967.22/985.77 req/s vs 878.88-1044.69 baseline, whole-window mean 951.56, F25/F26), while CPU steps 44.85% -> 90.0% at 13:22Z at unchanged throughput and memory shows no buildup (F27, F30). With H2's load-surge first hop directly measured and refuted, the two hypotheses no longer share the same observable facts; only H1 explains CPU doubling at constant QPS. (2) The redis trigger is no longer an unverified assumption: logs give a discrete event - redis-cache-2 failing 3 consecutive PING checks at 13:22:10Z and promotion of redis-cache-3 at 13:22:52Z with an explicitly EMPTY dataset (F34) - and 120s-resolution hit_ratio confirms the collapse starts in the 13:22Z bucket (95.9% at 13:20Z -> 10.82% at 13:22Z, F35), not in 13:16-13:20Z. That rules out eviction/memory-pressure as trigger (evictions flat 1.96-4.13/min F31, memory 65-75% then collapse to 6.0% F32, connected_clients 311->40 F33) and matches the mechanism in market-data-service's own logs (F28). (3) The 'no change precedes onset' claim is now robust: the partial deployment listing was re-run clean with the same count (F2), and exchange-gateway and order-service got individual zero-change/zero-deploy checks (F21/F22), closing the scope gap. Scope checks out: redis-cache is the only shared:true node on both ailing services' paths (F5/F23), exchange-gateway stayed flat at 127-136ms (F16), pricing-engine CPU flat (F12), so H3/H4 remain contradicted. Residual uncertainty is confined to a secondary detail - the sub-cause inside redis-cache-2 (OOM/host/network) and whether any redis host telemetry exists - which changes the deeper origin narrative but not the ranked origin or the fix (restore/repopulate cache, fix failover-to-empty-replica behavior). Confidence capped at 0.82: one hop (miss storm -> CPU saturation) is still an inference from co-timing rather than a pre/post controlled comparison, and the only evidence for the empty-dataset premise is a log line plus inferred memory/clients collapse (no keyspace_size metric exists, F37).

challenges.issue: The miss-storm -> CPU-saturation hop remains an inference from co-timing (F14 F28 F29 F30) rather than a controlled comparison; there is no direct cache-miss count series (F37, gap list). This is a real but bounded weakness: flat QPS + doubled CPU + explicit per-quote rebuild logs make alternative explanations for the CPU step hard to construct, so it warrants a confidence cap rather than more queries.

The empty-dataset premise rests on one WARN log line (F34) plus inferred memory_pct/connected_clients collapse (F32/F33); redis-cache exposes no keyspace_size/used_memory metric (F37), so the emptied-dataset claim is not independently measured.

Sub-cause of the redis-cache-2 PING-timeout failure (OOM/host/network) is undetermined; no redis node-level host telemetry exists. This is an origin-detail gap below the ranked hypothesis, not an alternative origin, and no available tool can fill it.

Metric bucket boundaries are 240s while the failover is at 13:22:10Z, so the '13:20Z bucket' onsets predate the discrete failover in bucket terms; only the 120s hit_ratio series (F35) and the 2-min CPU step (F14) constrain ordering. Strict sub-bucket ordering between redis and market-data-service cannot be proven.
